prize_parts.citation: for showing how borrowing limits tied to collateral values amplify and propagate shocks, generating persistent credit cycles in the macroeconomy

statement.case_for: I keep B006 as my first choice, but I now propose the two-name Kiyotaki-Moore version. The core discovery is a single mechanism: when borrowing is limited by the value of collateral, and collateral values depend on credit and activity, small shocks become large and persistent fluctuations (Kiyotaki and Moore, 1997). The mechanism is nearly thirty years old and has been extended and applied in a large macro-finance literature, including after 2007-09. It changed how macroeconomists model aggregate fluctuations, asset prices and macroprudential policy. All eleven round-1 files either prefer this core or describe it as the clearest attribution, and no member disputes Kiyotaki and Moore as originators. I treat that as a check on attribution, not as evidence of merit. The merit rests on how the mechanism reorganised a field's reasoning, on its maturity and on its durability. A narrow, mechanism-anchored citation also avoids the bank-run and deposit-insurance themes that the 2022 prize addressed.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservations remain the thematic adjacency to the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises, and the mixed empirical identification of the specific collateral channel. Evidence for financial-friction amplification in general is stronger than evidence for the Kiyotaki-Moore mechanism specifically. The theory's influence arguably runs ahead of direct micro-data validation. A two-name award also leaves out Gertler and Gilchrist, whose quantitative and empirical contributions are real. Since I changed my configuration, I should say that the case for a third name rested on my recollection of work I cannot verify here, and I could not name its separable contribution with confidence. Finally, B047 has a compact, traceable attribution and a longer applied record in antitrust, regulation and auctions. I have limited expertise in structural industrial organisation, so my relative weighting of B006 and B047 is the least reliable part of my judgement.

responses.point: Krusell's round-1 file prefers B006 with Kiyotaki, Moore and Gertler. He argues that Gertler's later intermediary-frictions work with Kiyotaki is a distinct extension after Bernanke. He also says the third name is an open question and that he would accept the pair if Gertler's credit proves too entangled with Bernanke's prize.
responses.response: I made the same argument in my own round-1 file, so I owe an honest account of why I now move away from it. The chair summary asks whether the intermediary-frictions strand is separable. When I examine it, much of the later work moves toward banks, liquidity and runs in intermediated economies, which is the theme the 2022 prize addressed. Other parts move toward unconventional monetary policy and quantitative monetary models. Those parts either rejoin the adjacent prize or pull toward the New Keynesian ballot, where Gertler also appears. I cannot name a clean, separable Gertler achievement without leaning on recollection I cannot check. You said you would accept the pair as a fallback, so I propose we treat it as the preferred configuration and not as a fallback. It is the version I can defend most easily.

responses.point: Friberg's round-1 file prefers a three-name B006. He keeps Gertler for the intermediary-frictions work with Kiyotaki, which he sees as distinct from the Bernanke-Gertler-Gilchrist accelerator. He wants the citation built on the collateral and balance-sheet mechanism and says he would accept two names as a fallback.
responses.response: I agree that the citation must rest on the collateral and balance-sheet mechanism and not on the accelerator, and my two-name citation is worded that way. On Gertler we differ in degree. The accelerator is clearly the overlapping part. The intermediary work is arguably distinct, but it sits so close to banking fragility that the committee would have to argue the separation in the citation itself. I would rather not build a prize on an argument that fine. Your acceptance of the pair is helpful, and I think it brings your view and mine to the same configuration without either of us claiming the third name is illegitimate.

responses.point: Strömberg's round-1 file ranks B047 first and B006 fourth, and proposes only Kiyotaki and Moore for B006. He argues that even with clean attribution, the 2022 overlap makes B006 less of a new step than a field with no recent recognition. He also notes that the evidence on the collateral channel is a weaker base than BLP's decades of applied use.
responses.response: I now align on attribution and part with you on weighting. I do not think proximity to the 2022 prize is a maturity problem, and I do not think it makes the discovery a smaller step. Bank runs and deposit insurance concern fragility within the banking sector. Kiyotaki-Moore concerns how collateral values propagate real shocks and generate persistent credit cycles. The chair summary asks whether we can apply one standard to B006 and to B023's overlap with the 2021, 2023 and 2024 prizes. My standard is that adjacency counts against a candidate only where the same discovery is already credited, not where a related field is. By that test B006 passes, and B023's task-based strand is the stricter case. Your point about the empirical base is fair, and it is my main reason for treating the B047 comparison as live and not as settled.

responses.point: Andersson's round-1 file ranks B047 first and B006 third. He finds the attribution argument for a Kiyotaki-Moore pair persuasive. He says B006 with those two names is the alternative he would most readily support, though he is concerned about proximity to 2022 and about contested identification.
responses.response: Your response addressed a two-name proposal that is not what my round-1 file contained, since I had moved to three names. This round I have reverted to two. That is the version you said you would most readily support, so I take your statement as a conditional that now applies. I agree that BLP has a cleaner empirical record, and I stay unsure how to weigh that against a foundational mechanism that organised a research programme. I would not call my preference decisive, and I accept that a reasonable member could place B047 ahead on attribution and maturity of evidence.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson's round-1 file ranks B047 first and B006 eighth in the opening. She credits a two-name Kiyotaki-Moore framing with making B006 a stronger alternative. She asks whether the empirical record supports the collateral channel specifically, as opposed to financial frictions in general, and says she would weigh it below a contribution that is both a method and a widely checked empirical practice.
responses.response: Your question about the specific channel is the right one, and I have no evidence to offer beyond what my file already concedes: the specific channel has mixed direct identification, while amplification through financial frictions is better supported. The disagreement comes down to whether a prize needs the specific mechanism to be empirically settled or whether it is enough that the mechanism organised and disciplined later empirical and quantitative work. I lean toward the latter, but I recognise that is a judgement and that you reach a different weighting on the common criteria. Your own account of BLP, with explicit assumptions that users probe through sensitivity analysis and merger retrospectives, is the strongest case for B047, and it is why B047 is my first alternative.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee considers the Kiyotaki-Moore mechanism sufficiently distinct from the 2022 prize on banks and financial crises, and whether adjacency should count at all when the same discovery is not already credited.
Whether the exclusion of Gertler and Gilchrist under a two-name award is a defect. I could not establish a separable Gertler achievement without relying on unverified recollection.

How to weigh a foundational mechanism with mixed direct identification (B006) against a well-bounded method with a longer applied record (B047). My expertise in structural industrial organisation is limited, so my weighting there is unreliable.
Whether B023 can be framed as one coherent discovery, and whether its third name should be Katz or Dorn.
All of my assessments of citations, usage and attribution rest on general background knowledge and have not been independently verified.
statement.conflict_note: No co-authorship or institutional tie to Kiyotaki, Moore, Gertler or Gilchrist is apparent from my profile, and dropping Gertler removes the question of whether any B006 name overlaps with other ballots. I disclose the following as collegial ties and do not adjudicate them. I am the chair and, as the chair summary notes, one of the explicit B006 supporters. I am an IIES colleague of Per Krusell and Timo Boppart and have co-authored with Krusell, Boppart and Richard Friberg. Krusell and Friberg also prefer B006. My own research field of macroeconomics is adjacent to B006, and I have tried to apply the same criteria as I apply to other fields. My 2018 presentation speech and the citation of my own work in the 2018 background are not tied to any shortlisted candidate. My round-1 file proposed three names and some responses addressed my earlier two-name proposal. This round states my current position as two names.
